entities.name: Ashoka the Great
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Ashoka Maurya (c. 304–232 BCE) was the third Maurya emperor, ruling the largest empire in Indian history. His transformation from ruthless conqueror to champion of non-violence after the devastating Kalinga War represents one of history's most dramatic moral conversions.

Kalinga (c. 261 BCE) cost 100,000 dead and 150,000 deported. Horrified, Ashoka embraced Buddhism and devoted 30 years to dhamma (righteousness). His Edicts — over 30 rock and pillar inscriptions, India's oldest deciphered texts — proclaimed religious tolerance, non-violence, animal welfare, and care for the poor.

He sent Buddhist missionaries to Sri Lanka, Central Asia, Egypt, and Greece — the first systematic international missionary effort. His four-lion capital at Sarnath became India's national emblem; the Ashoka Chakra adorns the Indian flag.

H.G. Wells wrote: 'Amidst the tens of thousands of names of monarchs, the name of Ashoka shines, and shines almost alone, a star.'

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Ashoka's transformation from a ruthless conqueror to a champion of non-violence had far-reaching consequences, including the spread of Buddhism across Asia and the establishment of India's national emblem at Sarnath. His Edicts promoted religious tolerance and animal welfare, influencing the development of Indian society for centuries.
